summary:
Saint Lucia decriminalised consensual same-sex conduct on 29 July 2025, when the High Court struck down colonial-era buggery and gross indecency offences as unconstitutional in Randall Theodule et al. v. the Attorney General of Saint Lucia. Human Rights Watch reported the judgment on 31 July 2025. The case formed part of strategic constitutional litigation across the Eastern Caribbean. For visitors, criminal exposure for private consensual adult same-sex conduct ended with that declaration.

Under Criminal Code No. 9 of 2004, effective 1 January 2005, as amended following the ruling, Section 132 defines gross indecency as genital acts other than intercourse for sexual arousal or gratification. It carries 10 years on indictment or 5 years summarily, but exempts private consensual acts between adults. Section 133 defines buggery as anal intercourse. It carries life imprisonment where committed by force without consent, 10 years in other cases, and 5 years for attempt or assault with intent, but exempts private consensual acts where both persons are 16 or older.

Before the court struck down the provisions, the buggery and gross indecency laws were described as unenforced. Statements in 2017 said no person had been imprisoned for being gay and that gay cruises, couples and visitors stayed safely.

A human rights sensitisation programme for enforcement officers began in 2014 for the Royal Saint Lucia Police Force on general and LGBT-specific content. Further training was held in Castries on 19 May 2015 for officers from the Royal Saint Lucia Police Force, Air and Sea Ports, Customs and Bordelais Correctional Facility, together with CariFLAGS, the Canadian HIV-AIDS Legal Network and Maurice Tomlinson, building on the 2014 work.

Two incidents of anti-gay violence are documented. In 2011, three American gay men were violently attacked and robbed in a vacation villa by assailants who used anti-gay slurs. In February 2019, 27-year-old Guyanese national Michael Pooran was stabbed to death in an attack attributed to perceived sexual orientation, which prompted public calls to denounce violence and discrimination and to re-examine the buggery laws.
tangentialFactors:
Saint Lucia was the only United Nations member in the Americas to formally oppose the United Nations declaration on sexual orientation and gender identity.

In March 2019, the United Kingdom Upper Tribunal decided that gay men face a risk of persecution in Saint Lucia and may claim asylum on that basis.

In March 2019, 17-year-old Gervais Emmanuel, described as openly gay, died by suicide. The death was attributed to homophobic bullying and pressure.
localsOnly:
Article 131 of the Labour Code, enacted in 2006, prohibits unfair dismissal based on sexual orientation.

The Domestic Violence Act, passed on 8 March 2022, extends all protections under the Act to LGBTQ people.
